cards.title: What makes a flame glow?
cards.idea: A flame is not a thing you can touch—it's a zone where hot gases and tiny glowing particles release energy from burning fuel.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see what a flame really is.

cards.reveal: A flame is a visible region of a chemical reaction (combustion) where fuel reacts with oxygen. The glow comes from hot particles and gases, not from a solid object.

cards.title: The three zones of a candle flame
cards.idea: A candle flame has distinct layers: a dark inner zone, a bright middle zone, and a faint outer zone. Each zone has a different temperature and role.

interaction.prompt: Tap each zone to learn what happens there.

cards.reveal: Inner zone (dark): unburned wax vapour and incomplete combustion—coolest part. Middle zone (bright yellow): hot glowing carbon particles—hottest and brightest. Outer zone (pale blue): complete combustion of gases—cooler than the middle.

cards.title: Why is the middle zone so bright?
cards.idea: The bright yellow colour comes from tiny solid carbon particles (soot) that are heated to high temperature and glow like a hot coal.

interaction.prompt: Tap to understand the yellow glow.

cards.reveal: Wax vapour burns incompletely in the middle zone, leaving behind carbon particles. These particles are heated to about 1200°C and emit yellow light. This is the same reason a coal glows red or yellow when hot.

cards.title: The outer zone burns cleanly
cards.idea: The pale outer zone is where leftover fuel and carbon completely burn with oxygen from the air, producing mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see what the outer zone does.

cards.reveal: In the outer zone, any unburned gases and carbon particles from the middle zone react fully with oxygen. This zone is cooler (around 300–400°C) and produces no visible glow because there are no hot solid particles—only invisible gases.

cards.title: Why the dark inner zone exists
cards.idea: The innermost dark zone contains wax vapour that has not yet reached high enough temperature to burn. It is shielded from oxygen by the bright middle zone.

interaction.prompt: Tap to learn why the centre stays dark.

cards.reveal: Heat from the bright middle zone melts the wax and turns it into vapour, but this vapour is still cool and oxygen-poor. It must rise and mix with air in the middle and outer zones before it can burn and glow.

cards.title: Three conditions needed for a flame
cards.idea: A flame only exists when fuel, oxygen, and high temperature are all present together. Remove any one, and the flame goes out.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see the three essentials.

cards.reveal: Fuel (wax vapour), oxygen (from air), and heat (from the reaction itself) must coexist. Blow out a candle and you cool the flame below its ignition temperature. Cover it and you cut off oxygen. This is why the fire triangle—fuel, oxygen, heat—is the basis of all combustion.

workbook.prompt: Which zone of a candle flame is the hottest and produces the bright yellow colour?
The bright yellow colour in a flame comes from tiny solid ________ particles that are heated to high temperature.
What happens in the outer pale zone of a flame?
options: Wax vapour is produced but does not burn
Carbon particles glow brightly and produce heat
Unburned fuel and carbon completely react with oxygen from air
The temperature drops below the ignition point
workbook.answer: Unburned fuel and carbon completely react with oxygen from air

boss.prompt: If you place a glass tube vertically over a candle flame so that the inner dark zone is inside the tube, what would you observe inside the tube after a few seconds?
options: The tube remains clear because the dark zone contains no combustible material
Black soot deposits appear on the inside of the tube because unburned carbon particles accumulate
The tube fills with bright yellow light as the flame moves upward
The tube becomes hot but remains transparent
boss.answer: Black soot deposits appear on the inside of the tube because unburned carbon particles accumulate

boss.prompt: A flame cannot exist without all three components of the fire triangle: fuel, ________, and heat. Removing any one will extinguish the flame.
Why does a flame appear to have a dark inner zone even though combustion is happening nearby?
options: The inner zone is too cold for combustion to produce visible light
Oxygen has not yet reached the inner zone in sufficient quantity
The wax vapour in the inner zone has not yet been heated to the temperature needed for complete combustion and glow
The dark zone is actually a vacuum created by the rising hot gases
boss.answer: The wax vapour in the inner zone has not yet been heated to the temperature needed for complete combustion and glow
